Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity
Volume, variety, velocity, veracity
Ownership, source, validation, risk
questions.explanation: (A) is RAVR, used to assess the data; these four assess the development process around the visualisation. Both are examinable and easily confused.

questions.stem: Under the risk criterion, the question to ask is:
options: Whether the source published its methodology
Whether the data contains duplicates
What the consequence would be if the figures were wrong, including reputational, financial, regulatory and personal harm
Who holds the licence to the dataset
questions.explanation: (A) is source, (B) is validation and (D) is ownership — all four criteria appear as options, so this must be answered on the definition.

questions.stem: Which is an integrity threat specific to visualisation rather than to data generally?
options: A duplicate record in the source table
Aggregating away variation that materially changes the conclusion
An unencrypted database backup
A missing foreign key constraint
questions.explanation: Also in this category: mixing data collected by different methods, and presenting modelled values as measured ones.

questions.stem: Poor data quality most directly constrains a visualisation by:
options: Limiting the choice of typeface
Preventing the file from being exported
Narrowing the scope of what can be shown and capping insight at the descriptive level
Requiring a different charting library
questions.explanation: Sparse or noisy data forces fewer segments, shorter timeframes and higher aggregation, with wide error bars on any claim.

questions.stem: "Defensive design" in response to weak data means:
options: Restricting who can view the dashboard
Showing ranges rather than point estimates, annotating caveats, and displaying sample sizes and collection dates
Removing all interactivity
Encrypting the underlying dataset
questions.explanation: Honesty about uncertainty is a design decision — a confident-looking point estimate on shaky data misleads even when arithmetically correct.

questions.stem: Which set of four terms forms the syllabus framework for bias in visualisation?
options: Ownership, source, validation, risk
Selection, response, confirmation, measurement
Accuracy, audience, data source, unconscious bias
Collection, storage, analysis, presentation
questions.explanation: (B) lists bias types from Data Science and (D) lists the pipeline stages at which bias enters — both are relevant but neither is the four-lens framework.

questions.stem: Designing a chart to please the executive who commissioned it is which lens?
options: Accuracy
Audience
Data source
Unconscious bias
questions.explanation: Audience — It manifests as selective inclusion, flattering scales and omitted context. Unconscious bias operates without that deliberate orientation, which is the distinction.

questions.stem: Bias introduced during collection:
options: Persists and typically compounds through storage, analysis and visualisation
Is neutralised by careful analysis
Affects only qualitative data
Can be corrected by changing the chart type
questions.explanation: "Bias is never removed by a later stage, only amplified" is the sentence to write in a 6–8 mark question.

questions.stem: A column chart whose y-axis begins at 92 rather than 0 is misleading because:
options: The colour scheme implies judgement
The chart type is unsuitable for the data
Column charts require a logarithmic axis
Bars encode value by length, so truncating the baseline exaggerates small differences
questions.explanation: A line chart encodes by position and emphasises change, so a truncated axis may be legitimate there if clearly labelled — the rule is about the encoding, not the axis.

questions.stem: Two series on independently scaled dual y-axes appear to track each other closely. The correct interpretation is:
options: The two variables are causally related
The apparent relationship may be an artefact of the chosen scales
The chart proves correlation but not causation
The chart is invalid because dual axes are never permitted
questions.explanation: (C) is the tempting half-right answer — the visual does not reliably establish correlation either, because the scaling was chosen after the fact. Indexing both series to a common base is the honest alternative.

questions.stem: Doubling the radius of a bubble to represent a doubled value:
options: Understates the increase
Quadruples the perceived area, substantially exaggerating the increase
Has no perceptual effect
Is the standard convention in bubble charts
questions.explanation: Value must be mapped to area. This is one of the listed misleading techniques and is easy to miss because the chart looks professionally produced.

questions.stem: Which misleading technique is hardest for a reader to detect?
options: A truncated y-axis
A 3-D column chart
Filtering — records silently excluded from the underlying dataset
A missing axis label
questions.explanation: Axes, labels and 3-D effects are visible on the face of the chart; excluded records are not. Filtering is the most invisible form of editorial control.

questions.stem: A chart shows strong growth beginning immediately after a slump. The technique to name is:
options: A cherry-picked timeframe
Aggregation bias
Simpson's paradox
Un-normalised comparison
questions.explanation: The counter is to show the full available series, or to justify analytically why that start point is meaningful.

questions.stem: A national figure shows improvement while every region individually worsens. This is:
options: A rounding artefact
Evidence of a data entry error
An aggregation effect consistent with Simpson's paradox, typically driven by a shift in group sizes
Seasonality
questions.explanation: The composition of the population changed. It is the strongest argument for asking what level of aggregation a chart uses before believing it.

questions.stem: A choropleth of total cases by council area principally maps:
options: Disease severity
Reporting delay
Testing accuracy
Population distribution
questions.explanation: Without normalisation per capita, the map largely shows where people live — which is why rates per 100,000 are the standard treatment.

questions.stem: "Reported incidents by suburb" carries which additional interpretive caution beyond normalisation?
options: It measures reporting behaviour as much as underlying incidence
It cannot be mapped geographically
It must be converted to ordinal data
It cannot be compared across years
questions.explanation: Passive and self-report datasets record the act of reporting. Engaged, confident communities report more, which inverts the apparent picture.

questions.stem: A 40-million-row dataset requiring live refresh, drill-down and per-region access control points to:
options: A spreadsheet dashboard with pivot tables and slicers
A presentation deck updated monthly
A business analytics platform such as Power BI or Tableau
A custom D3.js visualisation
questions.explanation: Spreadsheets fail past roughly a million rows and lack row-level security; a custom build could do it but buys flexibility no one needs here at a cost no one needs to pay.

questions.stem: The decisive weakness of presenting figures in slide software is:
options: It cannot render charts
It cannot include narrative text
It cannot be shared with executives
It is a static snapshot — stale on export and impossible to interrogate
questions.explanation: Its strengths — narrative control, speaker notes, universal familiarity — are exactly why it remains right for a one-off briefing.

questions.stem: A custom-coded visualisation is best justified when:
options: A novel visual form is required for a public-facing product that off-the-shelf tools cannot produce
The dataset is small and the audience internal
The team lacks developers and needs speed
The budget is minimal
questions.explanation: You are buying unlimited flexibility with development cost, timeline, maintenance liability and an accessibility burden a BI tool would have handled.

questions.stem: The characteristic governance failure of spreadsheet dashboards is:
options: They cannot compute aggregates
They require a server licence
They cannot be printed
Version sprawl — multiple conflicting copies with no single source of truth
questions.explanation: Alongside manual refresh and fragile cross-workbook links. Their genuine strengths are ubiquity, low cost and auditable formulas.

questions.stem: When justifying a visualisation tool, the strongest answer:
options: Lists the features of the chosen tool
States explicit criteria, evaluates the options against them, and explains why the alternatives are worse
Names the market-leading product
Describes the chart types each tool supports
questions.explanation: "Justify" specifically requires the rejection of alternatives — feature lists cap at roughly half marks.

questions.stem: The five syllabus moves for interrogating a visualisation are:
options: Slice, dice, drill, roll-up, pivot
Interpret, aggregation, filtering, outliers, reasoning
Ownership, source, validation, risk, cost
Collect, clean, store, analyse, present
questions.explanation: They function as a mark scheme in disguise for any stimulus question — work through them in order.

questions.stem: The first action when interrogating an unfamiliar chart is to read:
options: Title, axes, units, scale, legend, source and date before interpreting the shape
The shape of the data, then the labels
The caption's stated conclusion
The colour legend only
questions.explanation: Reading the shape first is precisely how truncated axes and un-normalised maps fool people — the shape is meaningless without the scale.

questions.stem: A single extreme value in a scatter plot can:
options: Affect only the median
Improve the reliability of the estimate
Be safely disregarded in visual analysis
Drag the mean, stretch the axis, and create or destroy an apparent trend
questions.explanation: Report the median alongside the mean, show the distribution, and state whether the point is an error or a genuine and important extreme.

questions.stem: Which chart title is strongest?
options: "Monthly sales by region"
"Sales fell 12% in the northern region after the July price rise"
"Figure 4"
"Regional performance overview"
questions.explanation: An insight-led title states the finding rather than the topic, removing ambiguity about the intended takeaway and reducing misreading.

questions.stem: UX and UI relate in that:
options: UI is broader, encompassing usefulness, findability and credibility
UX is the whole quality of the interaction; UI is the visual and interactive surface, one component of it
They are synonyms in current practice
UX applies to software and UI to print
questions.explanation: (A) is the pair inverted. A beautiful UI on a dashboard nobody can find an answer in is a UX failure.

questions.stem: Applying "visibility of system status" to a dashboard means:
options: Showing loading indicators and a "last refreshed" timestamp
Displaying the organisation's branding prominently
Using high-contrast colours throughout
Providing a printable version
questions.explanation: A dashboard that silently serves stale data after a feed failure is worse than one that shows no data at all.

questions.stem: Grouping related KPIs by placing them close together relies on which Gestalt principle?
options: Similarity
Continuity
Closure
Proximity
questions.explanation: Proximity — Similarity groups by shared colour or shape and enclosure by a shared boundary — using these deliberately reduces the need for heavy borders.

questions.stem: Tufte's data-ink ratio principle recommends removing:
options: Axis labels and units
Chartjunk — heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, drop shadows and decorative backgrounds
The chart title
The data source citation
questions.explanation: The principle maximises ink devoted to data; labels, titles and provenance are data-supporting elements, not junk.

questions.stem: WCAG requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text. For large text the minimum is:
questions.explanation: 3:1 — at AA. The 7:1 figure is the AAA requirement for normal text, which is the closest distractor.

questions.stem: Around 8% of males have a colour vision deficiency. The design rule that follows is:
options: Use greyscale only
Increase font size throughout
Avoid all use of colour in charts
Never encode meaning by colour alone — add labels, patterns or direct annotation
questions.explanation: Redundant encoding preserves the meaning for everyone without removing a useful cue for those who can perceive it.

questions.stem: Placing the primary KPI at the top-left of a dashboard is justified by:
options: The data-ink ratio
WCAG conformance requirements
Gestalt closure
F- and Z-pattern scanning behaviour in left-to-right reading cultures
questions.explanation: Screen position is itself a hierarchy decision, alongside size, weight and colour.

questions.stem: Responsive dashboard design requires:
options: Identical layout across all devices for consistency
Removal of all interactivity on mobile
Reflowed layout, fewer elements per screen and touch targets of at least about 44 pixels
Fixed pixel widths to preserve proportions
questions.explanation: A desktop dashboard scaled down is unusable — mobile layouts should surface the two or three metrics that drive a decision in the field.

questions.stem: Which is a measurable UX evaluation criterion?
options: "The dashboard feels modern"
"Time to locate a specified figure under 30 seconds; task completion at least 90%; SUS score at least 68"
"Users said they liked it"
"It uses the approved brand palette"
questions.explanation: Criteria must be defined before testing and be measurable — vague aesthetic goals can be asserted but not evaluated.

questions.stem: To find out why users cannot locate a figure, the best method is:
options: A satisfaction survey
Usability testing with a think-aloud protocol
Counting page views
Asking the developer to review the layout
questions.explanation: Analytics tell you that users failed; observation with think-aloud reveals the reasoning behind the failure.

questions.stem: Discovering at the exploration stage that a key field is 40% null should send the developer:
options: Back to sourcing and preparing data
Forward to design with a caveat
Directly to deployment
To a different charting tool
questions.explanation: The workflow is explicitly iterative — the loops backward from exploration and from testing are the point of the diagram.

questions.stem: Row-level security in a BI tool means:
options: Each row is separately encrypted
Users see only the rows they are entitled to see, enforced at the data layer
Rows are versioned individually
Rows are sorted by user permission
questions.explanation: One dashboard serving many audiences, which is far safer than maintaining separate filtered copies per team.

questions.stem: Before publishing a public dashboard of health outcomes by small area, the essential step is:
options: Converting measures to ordinal ranks
Restricting access to registered users
Suppressing small cells that could permit re-identification
Hosting the dashboard on premises
questions.explanation: (B) avoids the publication requirement rather than meeting it safely, and hosting location does nothing about disclosure risk.

questions.stem: A dashboard indicates "below target" using red text only. The correct remedy is:
options: Add a redundant cue such as an icon, arrow or explicit "below target" label
Increase the font size of the value
Change the chart type to a gauge
Move the KPI to the top-left of the layout
questions.explanation: Redundant encoding retains the colour cue for those who perceive it while making the meaning available to everyone else.

questions.stem: A board member insists every available measure appear on a single screen. The best UX response is:
options: Reduce all 40 charts proportionally so they fit
Explain that the request cannot be met
Show the three decision-critical KPIs with trend, and provide drill-through to detail
Split the content across 40 linked pages
questions.explanation: An executive needs to know whether to act, not to see every measure. Drill-through preserves access to detail without the cognitive load.

questions.stem: Total complaints are falling while complaints per 1,000 customers are rising. The correct reading is:
options: The two series contradict each other, so the data is unreliable
Seasonality explains the divergence
The rate calculation contains an error
The customer base shrank; the rate is the more meaningful measure of service quality
questions.explanation: Both series can be simultaneously correct — normalisation against a changing denominator changes the story, which is the point being tested.

questions.stem: A dashboard's "last updated" timestamp is three days old but the feed failed a week ago. The design failure is:
options: An inappropriate colour palette
Excessive interactivity
The system neither surfaces feed failure nor degrades gracefully
Insufficient chart variety
questions.explanation: Live analysis carries an obligation to show data health, not merely a timestamp that itself may be stale.

questions.stem: The strongest structure for evaluating a completed dashboard is:
options: Describe each chart in turn and note its purpose
State the criterion, give the evidence, judge, note the limitation, recommend the improvement
List the software features used to build it
Compare it against a competitor's published dashboard
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the most common way to lose marks on an extended evaluation question.

questions.stem: Blending live operational feeds with warehouse history on one dashboard enables:
options: Faster ETL processing
Elimination of the need for cleaning
Comparison of today's performance against the historical baseline, flagging deviation in real time
Automatic correction of collection bias
questions.explanation: "Today versus the same day last year" is possible only because the warehouse retains conformed history alongside the live feed.

questions.stem: A store-floor dashboard for shift managers should prioritise:
options: Maximum data density to avoid navigation
Removal of all filters to prevent misuse
A monochrome palette for print compatibility
Mobile-responsive layout, few decision-relevant metrics and large touch targets
questions.explanation: Design follows the persona and the context of use — standing, glancing, on a phone, mid-shift.

questions.stem: The most coherent pipeline for a recurring forecast dashboard is:
options: Spreadsheet → screenshot → slide deck
SQL database → ETL → forecasting model → BI dashboard
Word document → PDF → email
BI dashboard → spreadsheet → database
questions.explanation: Each tool does what it does best. The cost is integration complexity and more failure points, which should be named in a balanced answer.

questions.stem: A visualisation is accurate, attractive and unused. In an evaluation this is:
options: A success, since the figures are correct
Irrelevant, since adoption is not a design concern
A failure against the communication criterion — an unused visualisation supports no decision
A success, since it meets WCAG
questions.explanation: Adoption, task success and acted-upon insights are legitimate evaluation criteria, not soft extras.

questions.stem: Indexing two series to a common base year is preferable to dual axes because it:
options: Removes outliers from both series
Converts both series to ratio level
Makes relative change comparable without manufacturing an apparent relationship through arbitrary scaling
Reduces the file size of the chart
questions.explanation: It is the honest alternative to the dual-axis technique, and it makes the comparison explicit rather than implied.

questions.stem: Adding twelve filters "for flexibility" most likely produces:
options: Higher task completion rates
Improved accessibility conformance
Faster dashboard load times
Choice overload and inconsistent results between users
questions.explanation: Most users never change a default, so the default view is the product — which is why sensible defaults matter more than filter count.

questions.stem: The strongest evidence that a visualisation improved an outcome is:
options: A measured change in the target KPI against a baseline or control
A high number of views
Positive verbal feedback from stakeholders
Adoption of the organisation's brand palette
questions.explanation: Views measure attention; the KPI measures effect. Output evidence is not outcome evidence.

questions.stem: An analyst presents r = 0.88 as proof that advertising drives sales. The best critique is:
options: 0.88 is too weak to support any claim
The sample must be a full census
Correlation requires nominal data
Reverse causation is plausible — spend often follows expected demand — and seasonality or price changes may drive both
questions.explanation: Naming the specific alternative explanations is what turns a generic "correlation is not causation" into an analytical answer.

questions.stem: Which decision most improves credibility with a sceptical audience?
options: Adding subtle 3-D depth for visual interest
Citing source, collection date, sample size and methodology on the visual
Using more saturated colours to draw attention
Removing axis labels for a cleaner appearance
questions.explanation: Provenance on the face of the chart pre-empts the first question a sceptic asks and signals the analysis will survive scrutiny.

questions.stem: Refreshing a dashboard every second for a metric that changes monthly is:
options: Best practice for currency
Poor design — refresh frequency should match the decision cadence
Required for data integrity
Necessary for accessibility conformance
questions.explanation: Refresh rate is a design decision balancing decision timeliness against infrastructure cost and user distraction.

questions.stem: A stimulus chart has no y-axis label. The correct first observation is:
options: The colour palette is inappropriate for the audience
Without units and scale the magnitude of change cannot be judged, so no conclusion about significance is supportable
The chart type does not suit the data
The data must therefore be qualitative
questions.explanation: Stating what cannot be concluded is the analytical move markers reward — it demonstrates interrogation rather than description.

questions.stem: "Engagement up 250%" most urgently needs:
options: A different chart type
A statement of the tool used
A confidence interval
The absolute base figures and the comparison period
questions.explanation: Two to seven interactions is a 250% increase and commercially meaningless. Percentages without a base are a listed misleading technique.

questions.stem: AR or VR data environments are defensible when:
options: The dataset is two-dimensional and modest in size
Spatial context genuinely adds meaning, such as overlaying sensor data on a physical factory floor
The organisation wishes to appear innovative
A conventional dashboard already exists
questions.explanation: The test is whether immersion improves the decision relative to a well-designed 2-D view — novelty is not a justification.

questions.stem: The strongest reason to run an accessibility audit before public release is:
options: Legal obligations apply and inaccessible design excludes users from public information
It improves the colour palette
It reduces the dashboard's file size
It speeds up the refresh cycle
questions.explanation: Remediation after launch is also far more expensive than designing to WCAG from the outset.

questions.stem: Which best exemplifies exploration rather than explanation?
options: A polished infographic issued with a media release
An analyst cross-filtering a scatter matrix to find which variables relate before forming a hypothesis
A one-page executive summary
An annual report chart prepared for print
questions.explanation: Exploration is analyst-facing, fast, ugly and iterative; explanation is audience-facing, curated and polished. Confusing the two produces cluttered dashboards and shallow reports.

questions.stem: A regional manager finds a national dashboard useless. The best response is:
options: Add drill-down with role-based default filters so each user lands on their own region
Aggregate the data further to simplify the view
Build a separate dashboard for each of the 30 regions
Remove the national view entirely
questions.explanation: One well-modelled dataset with drill-down and row-level security serves many personas without version sprawl.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question on bias in a visualisation, the strongest answer identifies:
options: The misleading axis and nothing further
The software used to produce the chart
The pipeline stage at which bias entered, the mechanism, its effect on the conclusion, a mitigation, and a judgement
Every possible type of bias in the syllabus
questions.explanation: Naming the stage and the mechanism demonstrates analysis rather than description, and produces a natural four-paragraph structure.

questions.stem: The most defensible criteria set for evaluating an enterprise dashboard is:
options: Attractiveness, colour harmony and layout balance
The volume of the underlying dataset
The number of charts and filters provided
Accuracy against source, time to insight, task completion, accessibility conformance, adoption, and effect on the target KPI
questions.explanation: Measurable, pre-defined and tied to purpose — state them explicitly before evaluating against them.

questions.stem: The single most important action to protect data integrity in visualisation development is:
options: Selecting the newest available tool
Adding more interactive filters
Increasing the resolution of exported images
Documenting provenance, cleaning decisions and definitions, and validating outputs against an independent source
questions.explanation: Integrity is a process, not a property of the image — traceability from the number on the chart back to the source record is what makes it defensible.

questions.stem: A visualisation compares 2020 and 2026 survey results, but the question wording changed in 2023. The correct treatment is:
options: Show the break in methodology explicitly, or restrict the comparison to a consistent period
Present the series as continuous, since both measure the same topic
Average the two instruments to smooth the transition
Convert both to ordinal ranks
questions.explanation: (C) manufactures a continuous series from two incompatible ones — worse than disclosing the break honestly.

questions.stem: An interactive dashboard defaults to "last 7 days". A user concludes performance is declining. The interrogation move most relevant is:
options: Outliers
Aggregation
Filtering
Interpretation
questions.explanation: Filtering — The default date range is an editorial choice the user did not make and may not notice — the most invisible form of control.

questions.stem: A visualisation shows a forecast band widening into the future. This communicates:
options: Growing uncertainty the further the projection extends
That the underlying data is incomplete
That the model was retrained mid-series
Seasonal variation
questions.explanation: Widening intervals are the honest visual signature of forecast uncertainty, and separate actuals from projections clearly.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate response to a stakeholder who asks for the axis to start at 90 "so the difference is visible"?
options: Comply, since the audience needs to see the change
Comply but add a footnote
Explain that truncating a bar chart's baseline exaggerates the difference, and offer a line chart or an explicit difference chart instead
Refuse and provide no alternative
questions.explanation: Offering the legitimate alternative meets the real need — making a small but genuine change visible — without misrepresenting magnitude.

questions.stem: Sparse, noisy data most appropriately supports which claim type?
options: A descriptive statement with stated caveats and visible uncertainty
A precise prescriptive recommendation with a dollar figure
A causal explanation of the observed pattern
A long-range forecast with a point estimate
questions.explanation: Matching the strength of the claim to the strength of the evidence is itself an evaluable design decision.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question, the reliable way to lift an answer from average to strong is to:
options: Reference the specific chart elements, figures and audience in the stimulus in every point made
Define each technical term used
List all five interrogation moves
Recommend a different chart type
questions.explanation: Generic, technically correct answers that ignore the stimulus are the most-cited marker complaint across every module.

questions.stem: A dashboard aggregates results to national level only. The most significant analytical risk is:
options: The file size becomes too large
Variation between regions is hidden, potentially reversing the apparent conclusion
The refresh interval becomes too long
The colour palette becomes harder to read
questions.explanation: This is the Simpson's paradox risk stated as a design consequence — aggregation level is an analytical decision, not a layout one.

questions.stem: Which statement about accessibility and usability is most accurate?
options: Accessibility features reduce usability for the majority
Accessible design is generally a usability improvement for all users
Accessibility applies only to public sector dashboards
Accessibility and usability are unrelated concerns
questions.explanation: Clear labels reduce errors for everyone, keyboard operation is faster for frequent users, and high contrast helps anyone reading in sunlight.

questions.stem: A colour scale runs red → green to indicate performance. The strongest objection is:
options: Red and green have insufficient contrast against white
Red and green are the most common colour-blind confusion pair, and colour is the sole encoding
Diverging scales cannot be used for performance data
The scale requires ratio-level data
questions.explanation: The problem is the combination of an inaccessible pair and sole reliance on colour — either alone is more manageable.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to show both the distribution and the individual data points for a small sample. The best choice is:
options: A bar chart of means
A pie chart of the categories
A box plot with the individual points overlaid, or a dot/strip plot
A stacked area chart
questions.explanation: With a small n, showing the actual points is more honest than any summary — a box plot alone can imply more data than exists.

questions.stem: The most defensible reason to include a data table alongside a chart is:
options: It fills empty space in the layout
It provides an accessible alternative for screen-reader users and allows exact values to be read
It replaces the need for axis labels
It reduces the chart's rendering time
questions.explanation: WCAG expects a non-visual equivalent, and precise values serve analysts who need to reuse the figures.

questions.stem: A dashboard reports "average handling time" without indicating the number of calls. The interrogation move required is:
options: Aggregation — at what level and over how many records is the average computed
Outliers
Interpretation
Reasoning
questions.explanation: An average over six calls and an average over sixty thousand look identical on the tile. Granularity and denominator are aggregation questions.

questions.stem: Which is the best justification for a dashboard rather than a scheduled PDF report?
options: The decisions it supports are made frequently and require the user to filter and drill for their own context
Dashboards are more visually appealing
PDFs cannot include charts
Dashboards require no maintenance
questions.explanation: Justify from the decision cadence and interrogation need, not from aesthetics — a monthly board pack may legitimately be a document.

questions.stem: A visualisation developer discovers the source dataset's licence forbids republication. The correct action is:
options: Publish with attribution, which satisfies most licences
Aggregate the data, which removes licence obligations
Do not publish; seek permission or find an alternative source
Publish internally only, which is exempt
questions.explanation: Permission to analyse is not permission to republish, and aggregation does not extinguish a licensing restriction — this is the ownership integrity criterion.

questions.stem: Which pairing of purpose and technique is correct?
options: Highlighting a significant result — adding more categories to the chart
Telling a story — presenting all available measures at equal weight
Simplifying understanding — reducing cognitive load through pre-attentive encoding and removing chartjunk
Highlighting a significant result — increasing the number of colours used
questions.explanation: The other options all add visual load, which works against the purpose each claims to serve.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants one visual for both analysts and the general public. The most defensible advice is:
options: Build one dense chart with all detail available
Build for the public, since analysts can read anything
Build for the analysts, since the public can consult them
Build two views from one governed dataset — a simplified public narrative and a detailed exploratory view
questions.explanation: Relevance to the audience is a syllabus dot point — one artefact serving two very different personas usually serves neither well.

questions.stem: In an OLAP-backed dashboard, a user's drill-down returns instantly, but the figure is 14 hours old. The correct explanation is:
options: The cube is corrupted
Pre-aggregation buys query speed at the cost of refresh latency
The network connection is slow
The measure has been incorrectly defined
questions.explanation: Speed and currency are traded against each other — which is exactly why real-time operational monitoring usually needs a different path.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of a visualisation failing the source integrity criterion?
options: The chart omits its y-axis units
The dataset contains duplicate records
The figures come from an aggregator that stripped the original methodology and collection date
The chart was built in a spreadsheet rather than a BI tool
questions.explanation: Source asks whether the data is authoritative, current and transparent about methodology. (B) is validation and (A) is a presentation fault.

questions.stem: A dashboard shows a KPI improving while the underlying measure definition changed mid-period. The most serious consequence is:
options: The chart renders more slowly
The colour scale becomes misleading
The apparent improvement may be entirely definitional, so the decision it supports is unsound
The dashboard cannot be exported
questions.explanation: Definitional change is invisible on the chart, which is why measure definitions belong in governed documentation with a change log.

questions.stem: The most persuasive way to present a limitation in an evaluation is to:
options: Omit it, to avoid undermining the conclusion
Mention it briefly in a footnote
State it, quantify its likely effect, and explain what would be needed to remove it
Present it as a strength framed differently
questions.explanation: Balanced consideration of limitations is explicitly required by evaluate, discuss and assess verbs — and quantifying the effect is what distinguishes a strong answer.

questions.stem: An enterprise's visualisation team has no documented style guide. The most significant consequence is:
options: Slower rendering across the estate
Inconsistent encodings and colour meanings between charts, forcing users to relearn each one
Higher licensing cost
Inability to meet WCAG requirements
questions.explanation: Consistency is a usability property — when red means "bad" on one dashboard and "brand" on another, every chart must be decoded from scratch.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest concluding judgement in an extended response on a dashboard?
options: "The dashboard is well designed and useful."

"Assessed against accuracy, time-to-insight and accessibility, the dashboard is largely effective — figures reconcile to source, the key figure is located in under 20 seconds in testing, and contrast meets AA — but the national-only aggregation hides regional divergence, so drill-down should be added before it is used for regional resourcing decisions."
"Dashboards are better than static reports."
"The dashboard uses appropriate chart types throughout."
questions.explanation: Criteria named, evidence given on both sides, a specific limitation identified, and an actionable recommendation tied to a decision.

questions.stem: A treemap and a stacked bar both show part-to-whole. The treemap is preferable when:
options: There are many categories and a hierarchy to represent
The comparison is across time periods
Exact value comparison between adjacent segments matters most
The data is ordinal
questions.explanation: For precise comparison (C), a sorted bar chart beats both — area judgements remain imprecise even in a well-built treemap.

questions.stem: A visualisation is judged "effective" partly because users can complete their task in three clicks. This is an example of:
options: A measurable, pre-defined usability criterion
A subjective impression
A data integrity criterion
A chart-selection rule
questions.explanation: Clicks-to-insight, time on task, completion rate and SUS score are all legitimate, testable criteria set before evaluation begins.

questions.stem: The best reason to show sample size on a survey chart is:
options: It fills otherwise empty chart space
It is required for WCAG conformance
It allows the reader to judge how much confidence the differences shown deserve
It reduces the risk of re-identification
questions.explanation: A 40-point difference on n = 12 and on n = 12,000 are very different findings presented identically without it.

questions.stem: Which statement about interactivity is most accurate?
options: More interactivity always improves a visualisation
Interactivity should be added where the user genuinely needs to change the view, and defaults should answer the primary question without any interaction
Interactivity is only appropriate for analysts
Interactivity removes the need for good chart selection
questions.explanation: The default state is what most users will ever see, so it must stand alone — interactivity extends it rather than excusing it.

questions.stem: A chart's legend lists eight series in a colour ramp from light to dark blue. The likely problem is:
options: The palette is not colour-blind safe
A sequential ramp implies ordered magnitude, which is wrong if the series are unordered categories
Eight series cannot be displayed on a line chart
Blue has insufficient contrast for text
questions.explanation: Encoding choice must match the level of measurement — sequential ramps for ordered data, categorical palettes for nominal data.

questions.stem: A dashboard tile reads "97% uptime". The most useful additional context is:
options: The colour of the tile
The measurement window and the target — 97% over a month is over 21 hours of downtime
The number of servers involved
The tool used to calculate it
questions.explanation: Percentages compress magnitude. Converting to absolute impact is often the single most clarifying move available.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason to sort a bar chart by value rather than alphabetically?
options: Ranking is usually the analytical question, and sorting makes it readable without effort
Sorted charts render faster
Alphabetical order is never appropriate
Sorting is required by WCAG
questions.explanation: Alphabetical order is appropriate when the reader needs to look up a specific category rather than compare — which is the exception (C) ignores.

questions.stem: A stacked bar chart makes which comparison unreliable?
options: The total height of each bar
The size of the bottom segment across bars
The order of the segments
The size of a middle segment across bars, because its baseline shifts
questions.explanation: Only the baseline-anchored segment and the total are read accurately — which is why small multiples or a grouped bar often serve better.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to visualise the relationship between marketing spend, revenue and store size across 200 stores. The most efficient encoding is:
options: Three separate bar charts
A stacked area chart over time
A scatter plot with spend and revenue on the axes and store size encoded by marker area
A choropleth map of store locations
questions.explanation: A bubble chart encodes three variables in one view. The size encoding must map to area, not radius.

questions.stem: The primary reason to annotate a specific point on a chart is to:
options: Fill visual space in a sparse region
Direct the reader's attention to the insight and supply the causal context the shape cannot carry
Meet the data-ink ratio requirement
Satisfy accessibility guidelines
questions.explanation: Annotation converts an observation into an explanation — one of the three named purposes, highlighting significant results.

questions.stem: A dashboard uses seven distinct fonts. The most direct consequence is:
options: Slower load times
Weakened visual hierarchy, since typographic differences no longer signal importance
A WCAG contrast failure
Incorrect chart scaling
questions.explanation: Two typefaces at most is the working rule — hierarchy depends on differences being meaningful, and seven fonts means none of them is.

questions.stem: Which best describes the role of white space in a dashboard?
options: Wasted area that should be filled with additional charts
A technique for improving render performance
A WCAG requirement for text blocks
A grouping and hierarchy device that reduces cognitive load
questions.explanation: It works through Gestalt proximity — separation is itself information about what belongs together.

questions.stem: A monthly report chart is exported to a slide deck and circulated. Two weeks later a figure is disputed. The structural weakness is:
options: A static export has no live link to the source, so provenance and currency cannot be checked from the artefact
The chart type was inappropriate
The colour palette was inconsistent
The file size was too large
questions.explanation: Static snapshots are stale from the moment they are exported and cannot be interrogated — which is the fundamental limitation of presentation software as a reporting medium.

questions.stem: The most defensible reason to show a trendline on a scatter plot is:
options: It makes the chart look more analytical
It removes the need to show individual points
Trendlines are required whenever two variables are plotted
The relationship is plausibly linear and the reader needs the direction and strength made explicit
questions.explanation: A trendline on a clearly non-linear or clustered relationship actively misleads — and it should never replace the points (B).

questions.stem: A visualisation of survey results excludes "prefer not to say" responses without noting it. This is:
options: Acceptable, since non-responses carry no information
A validation error in the source data
Required for accessibility
A filtering decision that changes the denominators and should be disclosed
questions.explanation: Silently dropped categories change every percentage on the chart, and the pattern of who declines to answer is frequently informative in itself.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to include the collection date on a public visualisation?
options: It improves the data-ink ratio
It is required by the Copyright Act
The currency of the data determines what conclusions remain supportable
It reduces re-identification risk
questions.explanation: It falls under the source integrity criterion — a perfectly accurate 2019 figure may be entirely irrelevant to a 2026 decision.

questions.stem: A chart uses a logarithmic y-axis without stating so. The consequence is:
options: Readers will misjudge magnitudes, since equal visual distances represent multiplicative rather than additive change
The chart cannot be printed correctly
The axis cannot include zero, which invalidates the data
The chart type must be changed to a bar chart
questions.explanation: Log axes are legitimate for wide-ranging or exponential data — the failure is not labelling them, since readers default to assuming a linear scale.

questions.stem: An enterprise's dashboard adoption is high but decisions have not changed. The most likely explanation is:
options: The data is inaccurate
The charts are inaccessible
The refresh interval is too long
The dashboard reports measures that are interesting rather than actionable
questions.explanation: A metric that no one can act on generates attention without effect — which is why "what decision does this support" is the first workflow question.

questions.stem: Which combination best supports the purpose "telling a story"?
options: A sequence that establishes context, reveals the change, and points to the implied action
A dense grid of every available measure
A single unlabelled chart with maximum data density
A word cloud of customer comments
questions.explanation: Data storytelling is data + narrative + visuals, and sequence is part of the design rather than an afterthought.

questions.stem: A colleague argues that adding a confidence band "makes the forecast look weak". The best response is:
options: Remove it, since the audience needs a clear message
Retain it, because concealing uncertainty misrepresents the evidence and exposes the decision to unquantified risk
Replace it with a footnote
Widen the band so the forecast appears more cautious
questions.explanation: Presenting modelled values with the visual confidence of measured ones is an integrity failure, however commercially convenient.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest sign a dashboard was designed without a defined audience?
options: It uses a consistent colour palette
It provides drill-through to detail
It includes a "last refreshed" timestamp
It mixes executive summary tiles, raw record tables and technical field names in one view
questions.explanation: Relevance to the audience drives density, vocabulary and interactivity — a view serving everyone typically serves no one.

questions.stem: An enterprise migrates a dashboard from a spreadsheet to a BI platform. The most significant governance gain is:
options: A single governed dataset with defined measures, access control and scheduled refresh
A wider selection of chart types
Faster chart rendering
Reduced training requirements
questions.explanation: The chart types are the least important difference — the governance layer is what resolves version sprawl and conflicting numbers.

questions.stem: A public dashboard exposes a filter that can isolate a single individual's record. The failure is:
options: A usability problem
A performance problem
A privacy failure — interactive filtering can reconstruct identifying detail from an otherwise aggregated view
A chart-selection error
questions.explanation: Small-cell suppression must be enforced after filtering, not only on the default view — an easy control to overlook.

questions.stem: Which is the best justification for a static infographic over an interactive dashboard for a public health campaign?
options: Infographics are cheaper to produce
The audience needs one clear, controlled message rather than the ability to explore, and the artefact must work in print and social media
Interactive dashboards cannot be made accessible
The public cannot interpret interactive charts
questions.explanation: Justify from the communication goal and distribution channel. (D) is a condescending and unsupported claim.

questions.stem: A dashboard shows a metric with no target, no benchmark and no history. The most useful improvement is:
options: Adding a decorative background
Increasing the font size
Adding at least one reference point so the reader can judge whether the value is good
Converting it to a pie chart
questions.explanation: Comparison is what converts a number into information — the same principle behind pairing a KPI tile with a target or a sparkline.

questions.stem: In evaluating whether data quality supports prescriptive analytics, the key question is:
options: Whether the data is clean, granular and complete enough for the model's recommendation to be trusted and acted on
Whether the dashboard refreshes daily
Whether the charts meet WCAG AA
Whether the data is stored in a warehouse
questions.explanation: Prescriptive sits at the top of the ladder and demands the highest data quality and model confidence — recommending an action on weak data transfers risk to the decision-maker.

questions.stem: A developer applies conditional formatting so cells above target are green. On a table of 400 rows this:
options: Is always an improvement in readability
Prevents the table from being sorted
Violates the data-ink ratio in all cases
Helps only if the reader's task is to spot exceptions, and adds noise if the task is to read specific values
questions.explanation: Design follows the task. Formatting that supports scanning can actively hinder precise reading.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about OLAP's contribution to visualisation?
options: It improves the accuracy of the underlying measures
It removes the need for a data dictionary
It makes visualisations exploratory by supporting fast multidimensional navigation
It guarantees the data is current
questions.explanation: Speed of navigation, not correctness or currency — pre-aggregation actually introduces refresh lag, which is the trade being made.

questions.stem: A time series is plotted with irregular intervals on the x-axis spaced evenly. The consequence is:
options: The rate of change is misrepresented, since equal spacing implies equal elapsed time
The chart cannot be exported
The y-axis must also be rescaled
The series must be converted to a bar chart
questions.explanation: Non-linear or inconsistent axis intervals are a listed misleading technique and are easy to introduce accidentally from a categorical date field.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument for building a visualisation iteratively rather than in one pass?
options: It reduces total development time
Iterative development removes the need for testing
Exploration frequently reveals data problems and better framings that invalidate an early design
It guarantees stakeholder approval
questions.explanation: Discovering at step 5 that a field is 40% null sends you back to sourcing — the loops in the workflow diagram exist for that reason.

questions.stem: An enterprise asks whether its dashboard is "accessible". The most complete answer addresses:
options: Colour contrast only
Contrast, non-colour-dependent encoding, keyboard operability, screen-reader alternatives, scalable text and responsive layout
Font size and chart type
Whether a print version exists
questions.explanation: WCAG's four principles — perceivable, operable, understandable, robust — require more than a contrast check.

questions.stem: The most defensible response to "the data doesn't show what we hoped" is:
options: Change the aggregation until a favourable pattern appears
Narrow the timeframe to a period that supports the expectation
Report the finding accurately, state its limitations, and let the decision follow the evidence
Present only the measures that align with the expectation
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all named misleading techniques — and all three feel reasonable in the moment, which is exactly why they are examinable.

questions.stem: A visualisation development workflow places "define the question and audience" first because:
options: It is the quickest step to complete
The audience must approve the tool selection
It is required before data can be licensed
Every later decision — sourcing, cleaning, chart choice, interactivity — depends on the decision being supported and for whom
questions.explanation: Starting from a preferred chart or an available dataset is how visualisations end up technically competent and practically useless.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes a strong from a weak answer on visualisation in this course?
options: The strong answer explains the mechanism — why the technique produces the effect — and links it to the specific stimulus
The strong answer names more chart types
The strong answer is longer
The strong answer avoids naming limitations
questions.explanation: "A CDN reduces load" earns little; "cached copies sit physically closer, so latency falls" earns the mark. Mechanism plus stimulus is the pattern.
